extracted.intended_audience: readers and students of philosophy, classical literature, and moral reflection
extracted.subtask_description: Montaigne's essay-form reflections on virtue, exemplary deaths, pain, and what constitutes excellence in men, illustrated by classical examples and personal practice. Includes observations on composition and the use of true anecdotes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Self-sacrifice for spouse (Arria and Paulina)
rubrics_metrics.description: Arria stabs herself and gives the poignard to her husband with the words 'Paete, non dolet' ('Paetus, it is not painful'); Pompeia Paulina offers to die with Seneca, saying 'I will go along with you.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Presented as a supreme expression of conjugal virtue: selflessness that prioritizes the other's courage and reputation over one's own suffering. Example: Arria's act is praised as 'noble, generous, and immortal.' Anti-pattern: failing to share or to enable the loved one's calm in the face of death.

rubrics_metrics.name: Stoic acceptance and exemplary death (Seneca)
rubrics_metrics.description: Seneca 'really embraced his death, not only without grief, but moreover with joy' and counsels moderation of outward grief ('Moderate thy grief...that it may not seem as if thou lovest thyself more than my reputation'). He leaves 'the image of my life and manners' to his friends.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The ideal is to make death an enacted proof of one's philosophy: face death calmly, use the moment to instruct and comfort others, and avoid dishonoring the occasion with excessive outward lament. Practical note: provide consolatory counsel to survivors and be mindful of the example your manner of dying sets.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prolonging life for the sake of others
rubrics_metrics.description: Montaigne (via Seneca) argues that 'it is a testimony of grandeur of courage to return to life for the consideration of another' and that one must sometimes 'lend ourselves to our friends' by prolonging life when it benefits those who love us.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Judges prolonging life (or abandoning a death resolve) for the utility or comfort of loved ones as a virtuous, courageous act rather than a weakness. Use the balance of personal resolve vs. obligations to others to decide whether to preserve life.

rubrics_metrics.name: Be, not to seem — philosophy governs inner understanding over outward decorum
rubrics_metrics.description: Montaigne: 'She forms us for ourselves, not for others; to be, not to seem' and philosophy should 'govern our understanding' rather than ritualized exterior composure.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Priority is internal steadiness and the right orientation of the mind; do not sacrifice authentic moral state to an imposed external show. Anti-pattern: valuing theatrical composure over genuine courage and clarity of thought.

rubrics_metrics.name: Allow natural expressions of pain (vocal and physical) when useful
rubrics_metrics.description: It is 'cruelty to require so exact a composedness' in extreme pain; groans, outcries, and roaring that relieve or distract the sufferer are permitted. Epicurus (quoted) even advises groaning in effort as helpful to the body.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Practical acceptance: do not demand robotic stoicism; allow bodily and vocal expressions if they help bear the suffering. Constraint: such expressions should not indicate or lead to despair; maintain the soul's capacity for rational thought where possible.

rubrics_metrics.name: Criteria for poetic excellence — Homer
rubrics_metrics.description: Homer is praised as having produced the most excellent work: 'so well acquainted' with many things, a 'treasury of all sorts of learning,' original (no predecessor) and unsurpassed ('the first and the last of the poets').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Poetic excellence combines originality, universality of knowledge, the ability to instruct across many domains, and perpetual freshness (never glutted or disgusted the reader). Example qualities to emulate: scope, richness of matter, and enduring authority.

rubrics_metrics.name: Criteria for military/political excellence — Alexander the Great
rubrics_metrics.description: Alexander is commended for beginning great enterprises in youth, achieving extraordinary designs with small means, commanding authority over experienced captains, and possessing virtues like justice, temperance, liberality, truthful speech, love for his people, humanity toward the conquered.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Greatness in a political or military leader consists of daring enterprise, strategic skill, personal virtues, and a combination of personal merit with fortunate circumstance. When judging such figures, consider total effect ('in gross by the main end') rather than strict application of peacetime justice to wartime acts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Criteria for moral-political excellence — Epaminondas
rubrics_metrics.description: Epaminondas is admired for a 'full and equal virtue throughout'—innocence, humanity, moderation in battle (avoiding killing without cause, sparing friends on opposite sides), powerful oratory, and consistent private and public virtue.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The highest excellence is uniform moral integrity across all domains of life: public command, private conduct, and knowledge. Emphasize consistent conscience and humanity even in war; avoid extremes of scrupulosity (Montaigne notes Epaminondas's poverty as perhaps 'too scrupulous').

rubrics_metrics.name: Essay composition method — spontaneity and minimal revision
rubrics_metrics.description: Montaigne: 'I never correct my first by any second conceptions... I have a mind to represent the progress of my humours, and that every one may see each piece as it came from the forge.' He writes after 'divers interruptions' and seldom revises more than to vary a phrase.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Favor preserving the spontaneity and immediate voice of the first draft to represent the author's changing mind and humours. Minimal revision is advised—alter only for phrase variety, not to erase original meaning. Anti-pattern: over-editing that erases the progress of thought.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of true anecdotes as source material
rubrics_metrics.description: Montaigne suggests those fond of telling tales 'do not rather cull out ten thousand very fine stories, which are to be found in books' and that one who would make a connected body of them would 'need to add nothing of his own, but the connection only.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prefer collecting and arranging true events from books as material for writing rather than inventing; the author's craft is often merely the connecting 'solder' between true episodes. Practical advice: source authentic anecdotes liberally and focus on arrangement and connection for effect.
